- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

2	name: build-pipeline
3	description: Use to run a non-trivial feature, bug fix, behavior change, refactor, docs-only change, or feature removal through the full spec-to-ship pipeline. Use it as well to set a project up on live-spec, where it reads the tree, picks the setup walk, and runs it. Spoken: attach live-spec to this project, adopt or install live-spec here, onboard this codebase onto live-spec, found a new project on live-spec, update live-spec here. A tiny reversible edit and pure research stay outside the pipeline.
4	metadata:
5	  version: 5.0.0
6	---
7	
8	# build-pipeline — ship a change by the method
9	
10	> Part of the **live-spec pack** — the shared working rules (ask-never-guess · plain words, anchors trail ·
11	> one surface = one name · one home per fact · junior/senior split · checkpoints · the concurrent-edit
12	> fence · freshness · journal discipline · attic-never-delete · verify by deed · the human's gates · claims
13	> need primary sources · fix the class, sweep look-alikes · the door before code · prototype ≠ product) live ONCE in the pack's base skill, `live-spec-base` (v5.0.0), together with the
14	> settings ladder — this skill references them and elaborates only its own domain. Used standalone, this
15	> note is plain advice.
16	
17	## Words this skill uses
18	
19	**Where the paths point.** Two repositories are in play. A path naming `skills/`, `guardrails/`,
20	`scripts/`, `templates/`, or `tests/` sits in the live-spec pack's own repository,
21	`github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`. An install copies each skill folder into one place, so a path
22	naming another skill points to that skill's folder, beside this skill's folder. A path opening with
23	`references/` names a file inside this skill's own directory, beside this file. Every other path
24	belongs to the project under change, including `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`,
25	`TEST_MATRIX.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `JOURNAL.md`, `docs/prover/`, and `.live-spec/`.
26	
27	- **the pack** — the shipped live-spec method: its skills, its document templates, and its gates.
28	  `skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md` holds the shared rulebook and names the ten working skills.
29	- **host** — one project the pack attaches to. Each host holds its own spec, queue, journal, and
30	  `.live-spec/` folder.
31	- **the human** — the person who owns the product decisions. A taste call, a threshold, and a policy
32	  all reach them.
33	- **seat** — the orchestrating session that owns judgment, briefs workers, and reports to the human.
34	  This page also calls that actor the senior and the orchestrator.
35	- **worker** — a delegated session the seat briefs for bounded mechanical work, narrowed to the files
36	  its brief names. This page also calls it the junior.
37	- **wish** — one request as it was spoken, before the door places it.
38	- **door** — the intake classification that places a wish at one entry point: feature, bug, refactor,
39	  docs-only, or skip. It is decided before any code is written, and it stands apart from the wish's size.
40	- **work-kind** — the intake axis naming what a wish produces: product, infra, skill, or prose.
41	- **footprint** — the reach of one change: presentation-only, single-module, or cross-cutting.
42	- **tripwire** — one fixed rule in the door step that lifts a wish to a door whatever its casual label.
43	- **row** — one line of the project's queue, `ROADMAP.md` in this pack, holding one piece of work.
44	- **spec-delta**, also **the delta** — the set of spec sentences one wish adds or changes.
45	- **regression fence** — one sentence in a delta naming a neighbouring promise that must stay true,
46	  citing the existing clause it guards.
47	- **landing** — the act of one piece of work reaching the repository's shared truth as one commit.
48	- **lane**, also **train** — one build lane a session rolls through the pipeline.
49	- **the pen** — the single write-lock a repository holds. One lane at a time writes shared files under it.
50	- **departures board** — the status view read live off the queue's open rows. It names each rolling
51	  lane's step, and whom a waiting lane waits behind.
52	- **red**, used as a verb — a check fails and stops the work at that point. **Green** names a run with
53	  zero failures.
54	- **gate** — a check that must pass before the work proceeds.
55	- **architecture node** — one named unit in `ARCHITECTURE.md`. It carries one responsibility, owns the
56	  spec facts it implements, and pins them to the code.
57	- **seam** — the named boundary between two nodes, stating what crosses it and who owns the format.
58	- **checkpoint** — a saved point of work a session or a worker resumes from, written under `.live-spec/`.
59	- **norm** — an approved prototype frozen as the binding record of a surface's look and feel, kept
60	  under `docs/norms/`.
61	- **problem ledger** — the per-host file `.live-spec/PROBLEMS.md`, recording the workshop's recurring
62	  operational noise.
63	- **class hunt** — the search a confirmed bug drives before it closes. Name the defect abstractly,
64	  find every sibling of that kind, and fix them together.
65	- **compaction** — the station that removes redundancy from a document or from code.
66	- **shopfront** — the public README as the reader-facing front of a repository.
67	- **attic** — the host's append-only archive folder, `attic/`, where a superseded file moves.
68	
69	**The bracket codes.** `INV-`, `T-`, `E-`, `ACT-`, and `M-` codes index requirements in this pack's
70	own `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`. `PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md` maps each code to the criteria that carry it. The word
71	`SPEC` before a code marks that same home and names no separate series. `M-1` is the milestone gate
72	and `M-6` is the push gate. A **base rule N** points at the numbered rule N in
73	`skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md`; its own frontmatter states how many it carries. A **communicator rule N** points into
74	`skills/communicator/SKILL.md`. That file numbers twice: its behaviour rules carry an inline
75	`(rule N)` tag, and its writing-register checklist restarts at 1. This page names which of the two
76	it means each time.
77	Each sentence beside a code states its own
78	rule in full, so a reader holding this page alone can pass the codes over.
79	
80	## The pipeline in one line
81	
82	One pipeline, and steps 1, 2, 5, and 6 each invoke a named skill. The order is **spec → prove → architecture → prove architecture →
83	matrix → test → code → verify → commit & show**. A bug shortcuts to **bug → matrix → test → code** (citing the
84	existing architecture node it lands in). **Skip the pipeline only if ALL hold:** single
85	file · no new state / element / user-visible behaviour · an existing test level already covers the touched
86	fact (still ship a test; the order of test and fix follows test-author's small-fix path — red first by
87	default, and a one-batch fix owes the mechanical red proof). A skip still owes the door step's spec-backed-literal tripwire: does this edit touch a spec-backed literal or clause? A yes routes the docs and the test into the same session as the fix (SPEC INV-104). Anything touching visibility / layout / colour enters at the matrix step minimum.
88	Otherwise don't skip a step — the bugs that pass every test hide in the steps you skipped. (The private playbook repo's PLAYBOOK.md holds
89	the principle behind each step. This skill is its executable projection; keep the two in sync.)
90	
91	**The craft ladder — which craft's standards judge each step (SPEC INV-33).** Each artifact is judged by its
92	own craft's standards: **spec** — a strong product manager (the user's journey, the
93	product's words) · **prove / prove architecture** — the prover's formal-methods reviewer ·
94	**architecture** — a software architect (nodes, seams, one responsibility each) · **matrix** — a QA
95	automation lead deriving coverage · **test** — the same QA engineer writing it · **code** — a senior
96	developer · **verify** — the visitor's own fresh eyes, the builder's own view set aside · **commit & show** — a careful
97	release hand whose reader is the human.
98	
99	The delivery report's step accounting speaks in these standards. The craft each artifact was made under is
100	namable on ask.
101	
102	The craft takes the work-KIND's form (SPEC INV-22, INV-33): on a prose product the code step is worked as
103	a strong writer, on infra as a toolsmith. The ladder names the archetypes, and the kind says what their
104	standards look like in its medium.
105	
106	## When to run it — and where each kind of change enters
107	- **Step zero, before ANY tool call: name the door aloud (SPEC T-12, INV-16; base rule 15) — and the human hears the intake line back as the capture echo: heard · door · name · row · place on the map (communicator rule 12, its capture-echo behaviour rule; SPEC INV-27, INV-37).**
108	  - The intake line states size (a wish too big for its worth is negotiated in SCOPE — cut surfaces or
109	    split into stages, never a time budget or estimate; proposals proceed on the recommended option and
110	    are surfaced, SPEC T-15) · priority · door: feature · bug · refactor · docs-only · skip · work-kind: product · infra · skill ·
111	    prose — what the wish BUILDS, one kind per wish, scaling the FORM of every step it walks (the
112	    work-kind table at [references/work-kind-table.md](references/work-kind-table.md); SPEC T-16, INV-22).
113	
114	    The same line PLACES the wish on the product's feature map — **changes feature X · a new feature ·
115	    restructure** — spoken in the echo and written in the row's `map:` note. The map is the spec's scenario
116	    sections plus the architecture's nodes, never a third document. A restructure verdict queues its OWN row
117	    (refactor door if only structure moves, feature door if behaviour moves too); the re-carve happens only
118	    through the architecture step and its re-prove (SPEC INV-37). A same-version docs-layout pass rides one sanctioned light vehicle: the pass builds on a clean pushed base, locks the owner's decisions in a checkpoint first, and proves content survived by a word-token multiset check and a punctuation multiset check (SPEC INV-111).
119	  - **The same line reads the FOOTPRINT — a three-source impact read that decides the route (SPEC INV-128).**
120	    Beside the door and the work-kind, read the change against three sources at once: the spec (what
121	    behaviour changes), the architecture (which module owns it), the code (what actually gets touched). Name
122	    one footprint — **presentation-only** (touches what the audience meets, nothing behind it) · **single-module**
123	    (stays inside one owned layer) · **cross-cutting** (moves a shared law or several layers) — spoken in the
124	    echo and written in the row's `footprint:` note beside `door:`, `kind:`, `map:`. **The footprint composes
125	    with the door, never overriding it:** the door decides which steps run, the footprint decides how far each
126	    step reaches, and the door's guarantees always hold — a feature never skips the spec step whatever its
127	    footprint (SPEC INV-16). A cross-cutting change opens the full pipeline from step 1, its architecture and
128	    matrix work spanning every layer it moves. A single-module change runs the steps its door grants with their
129	    scope narrowed to the one owned module (its architecture read, its matrix rows, its tests bounded to that
130	    module's block and interface); a single-module bug or refactor takes the existing matrix-step entry, a
131	    single-module feature keeps its spec step with the rest scoped down. A presentation-only change takes the
132	    lightest road its door already grants — the skip boundary or the docs-only door where the door routes it
133	    there, and the matrix-step minimum focused on the visible layer where it is a visible feature. The
134	    footprint sizes the reach, and the wish's size does not — a heavy process on a light change is as much a defect as the
135	    reverse. When the three sources DISAGREE (a spec-promised surface with no owning node, code behaviour no
136	    clause backs, a node pinned to a moved line), name the disagreement and route it to its owner (a bug row, a
137	    spec fix, a restructure row — SPEC INV-37), never silently trusting one source; the three-source read is
138	    the verdict derive-before-fork (SPEC INV-121) rests on. The footprint **re-classifies mid-work** the moment
139	    an edit reaches past its named layer (presentation → single-module, single-module → cross-cutting), the
140	    delivery report recording footprint held or re-classified to X at step N — the sibling of the door's
141	    mid-work re-fire below. (The mechanical `footprint:`-note suite check [INV-134], the per-kind
142	    concrete-layers-and-proofs declaration [INV-135], and the cross-cut counter [INV-128 boundary-health,
143	    `guardrails/crosscut_counter.py`] have landed; the declared-module-interface and interface-level test
144	    machinery rides its own follow-on row; this step states the read and the routing.)
145	  - Tripwires decide by rule, ahead of judgment — a new user-visible surface · new persistent state · a new interaction on an existing surface
146	    · the spec marks the touched surface [target] · behaviour no spec clause backs ⇒ FEATURE, however
147	    casually asked. The tripwire verdict outranks a casual "bugfix" label, and queue-cutting belongs to the
148	    bug door alone — a re-doored wish takes no preemption.
149	  - Re-fire the door mid-work the moment the work is
150	    about to create a surface or state its door doesn't grant: STOP, reclassify, continue by the right
151	    door. When the re-door creates a surface or state that did not exist when the lanes opened, the same
152	    re-check **re-runs the independence edges against every rolling lane (SPEC INV-131)** — the new surface
153	    can collide with a sibling that was independent a moment ago; a new edge pulls the re-doored lane back
154	    to serial (waiting behind the lane it now shares a surface with) with a board line, so the departures
155	    board never asserts a stale independence after the ground moved. The integration re-fence [INV-39]
156	    still catches the collision at landing; this closes the board's observability gap and adds no new net.
157	  - **A declared mockup-first entry condition is honoured from the row, cancelled only by name (SPEC
158	    INV-43).** A story whose intake said "show me first, then build" carries the condition WRITTEN in
159	    its queue row ("entry: mockup-first"); a later general "go build" moves priority, never the
160	    condition — only by the human naming it does the condition fall. A condition living only in chat
161	    memory is the defect this line prevents (the tlvphoto door was built past its voiced mockup-first word).
162	  - **One wish = one user story (SPEC T-17):** a wish carrying several distinct things a person will DO and
163	    SEE splits at intake — each story its own row through the full pipeline (stages slice ONE story's depth,
164	    T-15's knife; separate stories never fuse into one row). Sub-behaviours (a hover face, a phone face, a
165	    backpointer) are the story's ACCEPTANCE, folded into the one story. Unclear whether it is one story or
166	    two ⇒ ask at intake, and every row born of a split cites the one spoken wish it came from. A request to
167	    merely SEE/TRY with no commitment goes to a labelled prototype home instead (base rule 16) — it stays a
168	    prototype, outside prod and unshown as product.
169	- **The door set is CLOSED, and a request enters at the highest document its change reaches (SPEC INV-151).** A request enters at the highest document in the derivation chain — spec → architecture → matrix → code → docs — whose sentences must change to satisfy it; the settings ladder stands beside the chain for a pure value. Walk the chain from the top: after this is done, would any sentence in this document read differently? The first yes is the entry layer, and the request flows down through every step its door grants. The set of entry points is closed — every request kind has a named home and a mandatory back-check, and a request the set cannot place is one plain question, never an improvised route:
170	
171	  See [references/request-kind-table.md](references/request-kind-table.md) for the full closed set of
172	  request kinds, their entry step, and mandatory back-check (product behaviour · a technically-phrased request · a defect · docs-only · a tiny reversible edit · a settings/parameter value · an inbox wish · a method/skill change · a sketch · research/a question · a feedback hand-back).
173	
174	  **A request that matches no kind in this closed set becomes one plain question to the human (base rule 1), never a guessed route.** The closed set is what makes "no gap between the layers" a checkable property held by rule, where before it leaned on habit: the landing contract already lists every door-granted step applied or stood down by name (SPEC INV-22), so a request the set cannot place is surfaced to the human as a question. This is the request-side twin of the property net's homeless-item finding (SPEC INV-150), the deferral test's (SPEC INV-152), and the earned message's (SPEC INV-189, INV-191) — one routing principle stated four times (SPEC INV-153): every incoming thing routes to the home whose declared sentence governs it, and a thing that pins to no home is itself the finding. The fourth control carries it across a window's edge: a message to another agent routes to the sender's own blocked work, and a question no work stands on is dropped and never sent.
175	- **New feature / new stateful surface / behaviour change:** the full pipeline from step 1.
176	- **Bug:** enter at the matrix step with a red-on-bug test (`bug → matrix → test → code`); if the fixed fact
177	  also lives in SPEC prose, update the spec sentence in the same change. **The door step adds one tripwire at the bug door:** does this edit touch a spec-backed literal or clause (a version string, a pinned count, a named vocabulary, a promised wording)? A yes binds the docs-travel-with-the-change rule and the red-first small-fix path into one duty — the docs and the test land in the same session as the fix; the tripwire reads the edit's content, so a one-word change to a spec-cited literal owes the same duty as a full feature (SPEC INV-104). **A confirmed bug drives a class hunt before it closes (SPEC INV-124). The hunt is four moves:** (1) name the defect abstractly (the KIND of mistake — a scope too narrow, a
178	  missing guard, an assumption that holds in one place and fails in the neighbour), then actively SEARCH
179	  every surface where that kind could live and fix all siblings in the same change — the search goes

501	## Guardrails — the pipeline's mechanical enforcement (every project inherits them)
502	The nine steps are guidance, and an agent drifts from guidance — that is the failure that stops a project
503	converging (a whole panel ships empty; a behaviour nobody asked for gets buried; a change lands with no test).
504	So the pipeline is not trusted, it is ENFORCED: a `guardrails` check the project wires to a **git pre-push
505	hook** (+ the suite), so a change that fails ANY of these is RED and CANNOT be pushed. `guardrails/` is a
506	directory of check scripts, and the pack ships one runner, `guardrails/pre-push`, that a project installs
507	as its own `.git/hooks/pre-push`. `tests/test_traceability.py`
508	(below) is the first of these — generalise it to the full set. **Each project INSTANTIATES the checks for its
509	own surfaces; the pipeline REQUIRES the check exists and is green.** This is a first-class step, applied across the whole project as a standing part of the method;
510	a per-project patch does not satisfy it. See
511	[references/guardrails-catalog.md](references/guardrails-catalog.md) for the four mechanical guardrails

462	   Beside them, a full audit runs on a landing-count cadence. It runs every ten landings since the last full
463	   audit [default; a host may set its own count on its word, SPEC INV-70]. At that point the pack reads
464	   the living documents whole, in the milestone gate's form (SPEC M-1). That whole-read is the full spec and
465	   architecture re-prove, the design review, and the doc-compaction sweep. It runs even where no
466	   milestone falls due, so a drift class nobody has named yet is caught
467	   before a human meets it late. The count is read from the landing commits in git history, and a
468	   milestone gate resets the counter since it already runs the whole-read. An audit is adversarial by
469	   nature: a whole-read that sets out to break the work, refute its claims, and find its holes (SPEC
470	   INV-46).
471	
472	29. **A deferral must justify itself, or the item is the seat's to do (SPEC INV-152).** A backlog item
473	   carrying a needs-the-human's-word marker is re-tested by derivability at its first writing and at
474	   every touch after. Three things carry such a marker: a queue row held for the human's word, a
475	   `NEXT_STEPS.md` line, and a decision a setup script leaves open. Where the answer pins to an
476	   existing artifact — a base rule, a spec sentence, the architecture, an approved prototype, or an
477	   already-answered decision [INV-59] — the item is the seat's: do it, cite the artifact, and drop
478	   the marker [INV-121, INV-143]. Where it needs a fact no artifact holds — a taste, a policy, an act
479	   irreversible outside git (rule 17), or the feel of a real device in the human's own hands — it is
480	   the human's, and the marker stands. Writing such a marker requires naming that human-only fact; a
481	   marker that cannot name it defaults to the seat's and is itself the finding. The posture is rule
482	   27's, applied to a backlog item, and it binds the orchestrator seat whatever tier holds it. Rule
483	   15's closed door set is its twin [INV-151]: one routing principle covers both, that every incoming
484	   thing routes to the home whose declared sentence governs it, and a thing that pins to no home is
485	   itself the finding [INV-153]. Two arms hold the rule. `guardrails/check-deferral-marker.py` reds a
486	   commit where a parked item in the resume file or a decision page names none of the four [INV-155].
487	   The deferral line of `hooks/chat-law-hook.sh` re-fires the test the moment a marker is written or
488	   an `AskUserQuestion` is opened; it reminds and cannot block (SPEC INV-28).
489	31. **Agents talk on exactly two channels, and a message earns its passage (SPEC INV-183, INV-189).**
490	   Several agents on one person's projects generate noise the moment they can talk to each other. This
491	   rule keeps the channel quiet while the necessary thing still crosses. An agent is a
492	   project window carrying its own tree, queue, gates, contracts, a standing mission, and a card of its
493	   own. A skill is a capability any window loads, and it dies with the session [E-31, INV-182]. Before
494	   acting on anything that might not be its own, an agent scans for cards and reads the owning agent's
495	   agent card, the `.live-spec/agent.md` in that agent's own tree [E-32, INV-184]. Then **exactly two channels** carry
496	   everything between two agents: the receiver's inbox for a one-shot request to change something, and a
497	   published contract for a recurring read. A reply rides the inbox in the other direction, so the count
498	   of two holds. Co-location changes the transport's speed and leaves the contract untouched, and a
499	   remote agent reaches the other through git alone [INV-112].
500	
501	   The laws below hold the quiet, and each is a way of routing a thing to the home that governs it [INV-153].
502	
503	   - **A message names the sender's own blocked work, in the message.** The named work is a real row, a
504	     real failing step, a real thing the sender cannot finish while the receiver's zone stands as it
505	     does. A message that cannot name such work is never sent. That rules out curiosity,
506	     tidiness, and the thought that a neighbour might want to know. Exactly
507	     two situations justify a message. Either the sender is blocked by the receiver's zone as it stands,
508	     or the sender has hit a fault
509	     in that zone and carries the evidence. The zone's owner is presumed competent and informed, so nothing
510	     that owner's own instruments already see earns a file [INV-189]. The mechanical check is
511	     `guardrails/check-earned-message.py`. It runs at the intake sweep and judges each deposit there;
512	     the sweep declines an unearned one at the door, so no human reads it. A deposit is recorded on
513	     arrival and never blocks a push (the owner's word, 2026-08-07 11:19: a request is written down,
514	     and nothing stands in the way).
515	   - **A referral travels back to whoever asked.** A question from another agent's zone is answered by
516	     naming that zone, and the zone's owner receives nothing from a referral. A human asker is answered
517	     in chat and costs one sentence. An agent asker is answered along the reply road as its message's
518	     terminal state. Forwarding a neighbour's question to the owner of its zone is the defect this law
519	     names, and the forwarder's own work stands on none of the answer [INV-190]. A question that pins to
520	     no artifact, and on which no work of the sender's stands, is dropped; holding it was itself the
521	     defect [INV-191]. A referral that points at a zone which does not own the question is named as a
522	     wrong referral, where the exchange loops back over the same pair. The two-crossing cap does not
523	     absorb it. `guardrails/check-wrong-referral.py` reds such an exchange on a fixture and rides
524	     the suite, staying off the push chain [INV-225, INV-196].
525	   - **Data never travels as a message, and a contract publishes nothing by default.** A consumer wanting
526	     numbers reads the neighbour's published artifact [INV-188]. Every field in that artifact leaves the
527	     producer's tree on the owner's explicit permission, recorded with its date and its author. How a
528	     neighbour's product happens to be built grants no permission, and a field with no recorded
529	     permission stays home. Credentials never cross under any permission [INV-185].
530	   - **An agent recognises a neighbour's zone on its own.** An agent may meet a fault or a lack in something
531	     another agent's zone owns: a rule of the method, a shape a neighbour ships, a field a contract
532	     lacks. It then scans for cards, finds the owner, and takes the channel that fits. The owner
533	     naming the road afterwards carries no fact the agent lacked, so his line is an acknowledgement of a
534	     thing already done. An agent that waits to be told has made the owner its router [INV-195].
535	   - **One question crosses between two agents twice, and the third crossing goes to the owner.** Every
536	     hop of a refer-and-re-send loop can pass its own law while the exchange manufactures traffic, so the
537	     bound is two, counted by the exchange's identifier. The third crossing is named in the sender's own
538	     status report as a zone question the two could not settle. The human-decision withdrawal loop
539	     already takes this shape [INV-196, INV-130].
540	   - **A concern no agent's zone owns goes to the pack, and the work never stalls on ownership.** A
541	     question no work stands on is dropped [INV-191]. A concern is a different thing: real work whose
542	     owning zone does not exist yet. It goes to the pack's inbox, and the pack answers who owns it — an
543	     existing agent, a new agent the owner ratifies, or a skill. Zones may overlap and no agent is
544	     forced to carve a disjoint one. The work never waits on the answer. An agent meeting an unowned
545	     concern does the reasonable thing now, in whatever tree can hold it, and marks that work
546	     provisional. The re-home lands later as ordinary pipeline work, cheap and retroactive, where a stall
547	     while ownership is settled is what this rule prevents [INV-197].
548	   - **A capability another agent's zone owns is taken through one of the two channels.** Building
549	     a local copy of a neighbour's capability is the violation the cards exist to prevent. The
550	     copy drifts from its original the day after it is made, and the two owners then answer one question
551	     two ways [INV-194]. An agent-initiated message stays a proposal until the owner ratifies it. An
552	     owner-initiated message is the one kind that carries the owner's authority, and relaying changes a
553	     message's carrier while leaving its authority where it started [INV-193].
554	
555	32. **A release's number answers what taking it costs a host (SPEC INV-217).** The number reports what a
556	   host that vendored the previous version must do to take this one. A **patch** fixes a machine to hold a
557	   law already stated: no new capability, no changed contract, and the host takes it and does nothing. A
558	   **minor** grows what a host may adopt in a backward-compatible way: a new capability, a new law, or a
559	   new gate. The host takes it by re-running its catch-up walk [INV-91], with nothing it already carries
560	   rewritten. A **major** is a release a host cannot take without changing what it already carries. Four
561	   things earn it: a reworded rule the host vendored, a renamed or removed surface a host depends on, a
562	   changed adoption or catch-up step, a moved law that forces host action. A major ships its dated
563	   `MIGRATION.md` chapter [INV-91]. The default is a patch. It is raised to a minor or a major only where
564	   the release earns the higher tier. This is a judgment the releasing session makes and states, **held by
565	   no machine**. The minor-versus-major call reads meaning a gate cannot, so it **stays a stated rule the
566	   session holds**, the same standing as a design-review finding that never blocks a lane [INV-141]. The
567	   2.0.0 release is the boundary case. Its migration chapter records "Host action: none", so by this rule
568	   it reads as a minor. It keeps its published number as this cited boundary case.
569	
570	33. **The authoring seat does not adversarially certify its own work (SPEC INV-237).** The seat that
571	   authored a change drafts and accepts it, and it never provides that change's own adversarial
572	   certification. A head marinated in the authoring context is blind to the blind spot it just wrote. Two
573	   carriers hold it. A release's adversarial pass — the full re-prove at the release gate [INV-116] — is
574	   authored by a fresh seat. That seat is a differently-contexted head briefed from the primary sources.
575	   It is the same freshness the verify audit already demands of its checker (SPEC INV-46).
576	   The 2.7.0 release ran its adversarial pass
577	   in the context that authored the new lenses, and so
578	   never turned a brand-new lens onto the skill body that introduced it. And a newly added lens or rule is
579	   run against the very document that introduces it before release, which is self-application, with the
580	   release record
581	   naming the result. A release gate may require a dated clean-context review record naming a seat other
582	   than the release's. Whether the review was truly clean-context is a process fact no gate fully sees.
583	   So the gate checks only that the record exists, is dated to the release, and names a different seat.
584	   That is the mechanical floor under a discipline the seat holds. The owner's word, 2026-07-18, after a fresh web
585	   review caught self-referential defects the in-context 2.7.0 prover missed.
586	
587	34. **A deferred item's own state is re-derived from the code before its work resumes (SPEC INV-247).** A
588	   resume file and a queue row record a past moment. The technical problem statement a deferred or
589	   queued item carries — how the code it touches works — can go stale as that code moves on. So the first
590	   act of resuming such an item is a freshness check of its own subject against the shipped source. Read
591	   the code the item touches, confirm the problem the row describes still holds, and re-derive the item's
592	   real current state before designing anything on it. It is the resume-side twin of rule 13's primary
593	   source and of the architecture step's pin read from a command just run. Rule 8 re-reads versions at a
594	   breakpoint, and the queue-take re-scan re-reads a deferred row's revisit trigger [SPEC INV-129].
595	   This rule re-reads the item's own internals. So
596	   a session never designs a fix from a stale model of code that has since moved, and an item already handled
597	   is caught before the work restarts. The owner asked the pack to hold it, 2026-07-20.
598	
599	35. **A session's record is read at both ends by an agent that did not live it (SPEC INV-302).** A session
600	   that lived the work reads its own record badly. Worked failure: on 2026-07-28 a session wrote its
601	   handover from memory. It named a question as still waiting for the owner, and the owner had answered
602	   it earlier that day. So each
603	   end of a session is read by a fresh agent. That agent works from a session extract: the person's own
604	   turns, each with its timestamp. `scripts/session-extract.py` pulls those turns out of one transcript,
605	   and its own header names where the transcripts sit and which traps a reader meets there.
606	   The extract goes to a scratch directory, since a transcript holds private conversation. At the close,
607	   the fresh agent writes the session handover from that extract. The session that lived the work writes
608	   no handover of its own. A handover is a file under `docs/handovers/` whose name ends in
609	   `-handover.md`, and it says where it was read from in three lines: transcript, extract, written by.
610	   At the open, a fresh agent reads the previous session's extract. It lists every decision the person
611	   made, each with its timestamp. It compares that list against `DECISIONS.md` and `NEXT_STEPS.md`. A
612	   decision missing from both goes to the seat before work starts.
613	   Both ends stay a discipline the seat holds. A script read the handover's three lines until
614	   2026-08-09, and the live-spec pack withdrew that script after finding no error the script had
615	   ever caught.
616	   A session's opening writes no committed artifact for a script to read. The owner asked for
617	   this reading as a standing process, 2026-07-28.
618

620	## Work that belongs elsewhere
621	
622	Reserve this file for the pack's own work: a session outside the pack uses a general style guide instead.
623	Never write host- or person-specific values here — those live in profiles, and this file holds only
624	package defaults and the rules themselves. The scope is pack-internal by the owner's decision (recorded
625	2026-07-16). The base serves the pack's skills and the projects that adopted the pack. It is no
626	general-purpose rulebook for unrelated sessions. That decided sentence closes the recurring scope
627	question for good.

629	## The settings ladder
630	
631	How the pack behaves is a **named setting** in one of four nested scopes. Resolution reads from the
632	narrowest scope out — **session beats host beats personal beats package default** (SPEC E-13).
633	
634	The ladder itself is one module in this same package:
635	[references/settings-ladder.md](references/settings-ladder.md), beside this file. It holds the four
636	scopes and their homes. It holds the package-defaults table every setting is a row of. It holds the
637	rule that a budget moves the pace and never the standard.
638	
639	Open that module when a setting is being resolved, proposed, or recorded, and not before. Nothing in
640	it is optional. Nothing in it moved elsewhere: the module is the ladder's one home, read on demand
641	rather than carried by every session that touches no setting.
